title: React Effects, Component Composition, and Lists
description: Understand when effects are needed, how dependencies control synchronization, why list keys matter, and how to compose a small API-driven posts list with loading and error states.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between rendering UI and synchronizing with an external system.
UseEffect to synchronize with external resources and understand cleanup.
Explain the dependency array and why missing dependencies can cause stale values.
Compose parent and child components instead of putting all UI in one component.
Render arrays with stable keys that identify items across insertions, removals, and reordering.
Build an API-driven posts list with loading, success, empty, and error states.

blocks.text: Rendering describes UI; effects synchronize external systems

A React render calculates what the UI should look like from the current props and state. Rendering should stay pure: it should not subscribe to an event source, start a timer, or perform a request as an incidental side effect. useEffect is for synchronizing a component with something outside React, such as a browser API, a subscription, a timer, or a request whose lifecycle belongs to that component. Do not use an effect just to calculate a value that can be derived from props or state during render.

useEffect accepts a setup function and a dependency array. After React commits a render, the setup function runs. When a dependency changes, React runs the previous cleanup before setting up the effect again. When the component is removed, cleanup runs for the last effect. The dependencies should include the reactive values used by the effect; omitting one can leave the effect using a stale render's value. An empty dependency array means the effect does not re-synchronize because of changed reactive dependencies, not that it runs before the first paint.

steps.title: Keep the current measurement in state
steps.explanation: The component displays width from React state. The browser's innerWidth is an external value that can change while the component is mounted.

steps.title: Subscribe after commit
steps.explanation: The effect registers one resize listener so the component can synchronize its state with the browser when the viewport changes.

steps.title: Clean up the external subscription
steps.explanation: The returned function removes the same listener. Cleanup prevents the effect from leaving a stale subscription when it is replaced or the component is removed.

steps.title: Render from the updated value
steps.explanation: setWidth schedules a render with the new width. The JSX stays declarative rather than manually changing the paragraph's DOM text.

blocks.text: The dependency array is not a performance wish list. It describes the reactive values that determine the effect's setup. When an effect reads a prop or state value, include it in the dependency list unless the code is deliberately structured so it is not reactive. If adding a dependency causes repeated work, first inspect the effect's purpose and how values/functions are created rather than suppressing the lint rule without understanding why.

blocks.title: Do not mirror derived state in an effect without a reason
blocks.text: If fullName can be calculated from firstName and lastName during rendering, it usually does not need its own state plus an effect that updates it. Extra duplicated state creates timing and consistency problems. Use effects for synchronization with external systems, not as a default place to calculate values.

Composition means combining small components that each express one coherent responsibility. A parent can own data and pass only the information or callbacks a child needs. Prop drilling describes passing props through several intermediate components that do not use them themselves. A few layers of props are normal and explicit; when many unrelated components need the same cross-cutting data, consider whether context or a state-management pattern is justified. Do not add global state just because passing a single prop feels inconvenient.

blocks.caption: Separate page, list, and item responsibilities

blocks.text: When rendering an array, React needs a key to identify each sibling item across renders. A stable key lets React match the same logical item when the array changes. Use a stable ID from the data where possible. Array indexes can produce confusing state or DOM associations when items are inserted, removed, sorted, or reordered. Keys are for React's reconciliation; they are not automatically passed into the component as a prop.

blocks.caption: Use a stable identifier as the key

blocks.text: An API-driven list has explicit request states

A list loaded from an API has more states than just “posts or no posts”. Before the response arrives it is loading. On success the result may have items or be empty. On failure the user needs an error state and a way to retry. Treat these states intentionally, and ensure a previous request cannot overwrite the result of a newer request after a query or component lifecycle changes.

steps.title: Model request states as distinct alternatives
steps.explanation: The discriminated union makes loading, success, and error separate states. TypeScript can narrow state by checking status and prevent using posts before success.

steps.title: Start the request and prepare cancellation
steps.explanation: The effect owns an AbortController for this request. It sets loading when setup runs and passes the signal to fetch.

steps.title: Check HTTP and parse the body
steps.explanation: The response status is checked before JSON parsing. A type assertion indicates what the example expects, but it does not validate an untrusted response body at runtime.

steps.title: Ignore an intentional abort and handle other failures
steps.explanation: Cleanup aborts the request. The catch handler avoids replacing state with an error after that abort; other failures move the UI to its error state.

steps.title: Cleanup and render by state
steps.explanation: The effect returns the abort cleanup. The component renders loading, error, empty, or success explicitly, and successful results render a list with stable keys.

blocks.title: Development may run effects more than once
blocks.text: React Strict Mode can re-run effect setup and cleanup in development to help expose unsafe side effects. Build effects with correct cleanup and idempotent behavior instead of relying on a particular number of development executions.

blocks.prompt: What is the intended role of useEffect in a React component?

options.text: Synchronize with an external system after React commits UI
options.feedback: Effects are for synchronization with browser APIs, subscriptions, timers, network operations, or other external systems.

options.text: Replace all event handlers and all ordinary calculations
options.feedback: Event handlers handle interactions, and values derived from props/state can usually be calculated during render.

options.text: Guarantee that an API request happens exactly once in every environment
options.feedback: Effects can be re-run in development or when dependencies change; cleanup and idempotence matter.

options.text: Allow a component to mutate DOM arbitrarily during render
options.feedback: Rendering should describe UI; useEffect synchronizes with external systems after commit when needed.

blocks.explanation: Use effects for external synchronization, not as a general place to move every calculation or interaction.

blocks.prompt: Using an array index as a key is always safe if a list is rendered with map.

options.feedback: Indexes can identify the wrong logical item after insertion, removal, or reordering.
A stable data identifier is preferred when the collection can change; keys help React preserve item identity across renders.

blocks.explanation: The key represents item identity, not just its temporary position in an array.

blocks.prompt: Which practices are appropriate for an API-driven React list? Select all that apply.

options.text: Represent loading, success, and failure explicitly
options.feedback: Separate states let the UI show the correct message and actions for each request outcome.

options.text: Use stable item keys when rendering the returned list
options.feedback: Stable keys help React match logical items between renders.

options.text: Use an effect to copy every derived value into separate state
options.feedback: Duplicating derivable data adds synchronization complexity; calculate derived values during render unless there is a specific reason not to.

options.text: Ignore every request error because an empty list looks the same
options.feedback: An empty successful response and a failed request have different meanings and should be represented separately.

blocks.explanation: Good API-driven interfaces preserve the distinction between pending, successful-but-empty, successful-with-data, and failed requests.

The request lifecycle has cleanup and avoids applying results after abort.
Empty and failed results are not presented as the same state.

items: Rendering should stay pure; effects synchronize with external systems after commit.
The dependency array describes reactive values used by an effect, and cleanup ends the previous synchronization.
Compose components around clear responsibilities and pass only the props they need.
Stable keys identify list items across changes; they are not ordinary props.
Represent loading, success, empty and error states explicitly when fetching data.

blocks.text: Deep dive: effect lifecycle, request races, and stable list identity

An Effect synchronizes a committed render with an external system; it is not a default place to calculate values that can be derived during render. React runs cleanup for the previous Effect before setting up the next one when dependencies change, and on unmount. Every reactive value read by the Effect belongs in its dependency model. For requests, cleanup/cancellation and stale-result protection prevent a slow response for an old prop from overwriting the current screen.

steps.title: Create one controller for this Effect instance
steps.explanation: When userId changes, React cleans up the old Effect instance and runs a new setup. The new controller represents the new request lifecycle.

steps.title: Check HTTP status and parse the response
steps.explanation: Fetch does not reject solely for status 404/500, so response.ok must be checked. The body is parsed asynchronously and state is updated only while this request is still current.

steps.title: Ignore cancellation without hiding real failures
steps.explanation: Abort is expected during cleanup and should not appear as a user-facing failure. Other errors still produce an error state while this Effect instance is current.

steps.title: Clean up when inputs change or the component unmounts
steps.explanation: Abort asks Fetch to stop and ignore prevents a stale continuation from updating state. Including userId expresses the reactive input that starts a new request.

items: Missing dependencies can leave an Effect using a stale closure; adding dependencies may reveal that the synchronization logic needs redesign rather than a lint suppression.
An empty dependency array means the Effect does not re-run for later prop changes; it does not mean the callback is guaranteed to run only once in every development environment.
Derived values such as `visibleItems = items.filter(...)` normally belong in render, not in state synchronized by an Effect.

List keys identify item identity across insertions, deletions, and reordering. Array indices are risky keys when items can move or be removed because component state can become attached to the wrong item.

blocks.title: Cleanup does not mean every Effect is wrong
blocks.text: Effects are appropriate for synchronizing subscriptions, timers, browser APIs and network requests. Avoid using them to mirror props into state or calculate a value that can be computed from current props/state. When setup is repeated in development, the setup/cleanup pair should remain correct and reversible.

blocks.prompt: A user switches quickly from `/users/1` to `/users/2`. Which design prevents a late response for user 1 from replacing user 2 on screen?

options.text: Fetch during render so the latest render always wins
options.feedback: Fetching during render repeats work during rendering and does not provide a reliable race-control mechanism.

options.text: Use Effect cleanup to abort/ignore the previous request and update state only for the current request
options.feedback: Cancellation reduces unnecessary work, while a freshness/ignore guard protects state from a late continuation.

options.text: Remove userId from the dependency list
options.feedback: That can leave the Effect synchronized to an old user ID instead of the current route.

options.text: Use array index as the key for the user page
options.feedback: Keys identify list items; they do not control network response ordering.

blocks.explanation: Request lifecycle and rendering identity are different concerns; use cleanup/freshness control for asynchronous work.

blocks.title: Fix an Effect race and an unstable list
blocks.context: Run this in a React project. The lesson sandbox does not compile TSX, so use the checklist to review your implementation in the app.
instructions: Implement user loading that re-runs when userId changes.
Check response.ok and separate loading, success and error states.
Cancel or ignore the old request in Effect cleanup and do not surface AbortError as a normal failure.
Replace index keys with stable IDs in a list that can be sorted, filtered or deleted.
Move purely derived display data out of Effect-managed state.
requirements: Every reactive dependency used by the Effect is declared.
Previous request work is cancelled/ignored during cleanup.
HTTP status failures and abort cancellations are handled differently.
List keys are stable identifiers from the data where available.
Derived display values are computed from current props/state instead of duplicated state.
hints: Read every variable referenced inside the Effect and decide whether it is reactive.
Use AbortController for Fetch and an ignore/freshness guard for state updates.
Use the item's stable id for key; index does not represent identity after reordering.
successCriteria: Changing userId starts synchronization for the new user.
Old results cannot overwrite the current user's UI.
Reordered/deleted list items retain the correct component identity.
Derived data is not duplicated into state without a reason.

items: Effects synchronize with external systems; derived values usually belong in render.
Cleanup is required when the old synchronization must stop or be undone.
Protect asynchronous state from stale results and use stable keys to preserve item identity.
